title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation attack, not a failure of a deployed AI product from a legitimate company. Scammers used AI tools to generate a fabricated news article featuring the likenesses and names of real public figures, including a finance presenter and a central bank governor, endorsing a cryptocurrency platform that does not hold a financial services licence. The AI-generated content was convincing enough to serve as the entry point of a multi-stage fraud, followed by scripted calls and small payments designed to build trust before larger sums were sought.

The failure mode is deepfake-enabled impersonation deployed outside any legitimate platform's control. It happened at the content-distribution layer, where fabricated articles and advertisements circulate through ordinary online channels before any regulatory or platform review can flag them. Catching it earlier would have required either automated detection of synthetic media at the point of publication or faster take-down coordination between platforms and regulators, neither of which is consistently in place.

What is not established is the identity or location of the people responsible, the total financial harm caused to victims, or whether any individual investor was defrauded specifically by the Alan Kohler article as opposed to related scam infrastructure.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing a fraudulent cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven has become a prominent example of AI-generated investment scams. The fabricated interview, which never occurred, depicted an increasingly heated conversation where Bullock allegedly stormed out over Kohler's questions about the unlicensed trading platform. This type of scam is rising rapidly, with Australian Securities and Investments Commission research showing that deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians are becoming more prevalent and convincing thanks to artificial intelligence technology.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase, including a 279 percent jump in phishing scams and a 151 percent increase in fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, along with politicians and financial figures like Pauline Hanson and Tom Piotrowski, top the list of commonly impersonated Australians. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, fabricated testimonials, and advertisements to lure investors, often followed by scripted phone calls and small payments to build trust. ASIC recommends verifying Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing.
